articles.title: Three different things people mean by verifying an audit log
articles.excerpt: “Verify the audit log” sounds like one task. In practice, it can mean at least three different checks: whether an application accepts a signed bundle, whether the chain of entries is internally consis…
articles.body: “Verify the audit log” sounds like one task. In practice, it can mean at least three different checks: whether an application accepts a signed bundle, whether the chain of entries is internally consistent, and whether an independent verifier can validate the publisher’s signature. Those checks are related, but they are not interchangeable. Conflating them produces reports that sound stronger than the evidence. What the recorded QA run showed A recorded QA run of our gateway exercised the distinction. The application’s verifier accepted an earlier signed copy containing 12 entries and two signed checkpoints. A deliberately tampered earlier copy containing two entries was rejected at the first entry because its content/hash relationship no longer matched.

articles.body: A failed render ought to look like a failure: a rejected promise, an exception, something in the console. With pdf.js on an oversized page it does not. The promise resolves, the code after await runs, and the canvas you hand to the next step is empty. All numbers below come from one machine (Apple M4, desktop Chromium 149.0.7827.55, pdfjs-dist 4.4.168), single runs, on a blank vector page I generated myself. Other browsers and phones have different limits, and I did not test them. What the render call reported The page was 14400 × 14400 pt. I rendered it at four scales and read pixels back from the canvas afterwards. At scale 0.5 (7200 × 7200) and scale 1 (14400 × 14400) the top-middle pixel was opaque white, as expected.

articles.title: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy Baseline: 3 Mistakes That Break Isolation
articles.excerpt: Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud A team applies a default-deny policy to a staging namespace on Friday afternoon, and within seconds every pod starts logging "temporary failure in name resolutio…
articles.body: Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud A team applies a default-deny policy to a staging namespace on Friday afternoon, and within seconds every pod starts logging "temporary failure in name resolution". Or the opposite happens: the policy applies cleanly, nothing breaks, and nothing is actually blocked either. A NetworkPolicy baseline sounds like a simple YAML exercise, but the documented behavior has enough sharp edges that the same few mistakes keep appearing. This retrospective walks through those mistakes as patterns, not as a report of any specific outage. Context: what a NetworkPolicy baseline is supposed to do By default, Kubernetes pods accept traffic from any other pod in the cluster and can reach any destination. Namespaces are an organizational boundary, not a network one.

articles.body: We Checked 514 Paid Backlinks Overnight. 11.7% Were Flagged. But 93 of the 95 link-related findings weren't deleted links. The anchor text had changed. Note on naming: The client brands in this article are anonymised as Brand A through Brand I . The architecture, the checks and the numbers are from the production system. Publisher domains are left as-is, because they're public sites and they make the failure modes concrete. TL;DR 514 paid placements are checked every night , automatically. On one night, 60 of them — 11.7% — were flagged. The failure is almost never a deleted link. It is rewritten anchor text: 93 of the 95 link failures were the phrase around the link changing, not the link itself.

articles.excerpt: I run a travel directory: about 800 prerendered pages, 190 redirect rules built up over a year of renames, and a small database behind it. For its whole life the front end lived on Vercel's free Hobby…
articles.body: I run a travel directory: about 800 prerendered pages, 190 redirect rules built up over a year of renames, and a small database behind it. For its whole life the front end lived on Vercel's free Hobby plan. Two things ended that this week. The first was an email saying I'd used 75% of my deployment storage. The second was something I'd been putting off: Hobby is for non-commercial use, and this site earns affiliate commission, so it never really belonged there. Paying $20 a month wasn't justified yet. Cloudflare Workers has a free tier that serves static files without charging for them, and the worker itself gets 100,000 requests a day. The site was averaging about 16,000. I expected a settings job. Point the build at a new host, copy a config file across, change two DNS records.

With his background performing Shakespeare and his incredible sense of dignity and gravitas, Stewart is being celebrated primarily for his work as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation , as well as being the perfect man to portray Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 31, 2015: Creepy skull-shaped Halloween asteroid flies by Earth, NASA names it the 'Great Pumpkin'
articles.excerpt: On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. Here's why it was so creepy.
articles.body: On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. It arrived with excellent timing on Halloween, which made the already-creepy asteroid even creepier. During its closest approach, the creepy asteroid was about 300,000 miles from Earth, or 1.3 times the average distance between Earth and the moon . So, it didn't pose a threat to our planet. It was discovered by astronomers at Hawaii's Pan-STARRS observatory only three weeks before the flyby, and it was given the official designation "2015 TB145." But no one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.

articles.title: The moon, Mars, and Jupiter shine in the heart of the Lion overnight on Nov. 1-2
articles.excerpt: The waning moon shines with Jupiter, Mars and the brilliant star Regulus in the eastern sky overnight Nov. 1-2.
articles.body: The moon dives towards the glowing heart of the constellation Leo for a spectacular rendezvous with Mars and Jupiter overnight on Nov. 1-2, as the glittering stars of the Beehive Cluster shine nearby. Here's what you need to know. Look to the eastern horizon an hour after midnight to see the 45%-lit waning moon shining less than 5 degrees from the red light of Mars — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length to the night sky. Jupiter's bright light will gleam just below the red planet, with the bright star Regulus lining up beyond to form a dazzling procession leading back to the horizon. The stars of the Beehive Cluster (M44) can be found twinkling 10 degrees from the unlit side of the lunar disk around this time, in the middle of the constellation Cancer .

articles.body: Something spooky is stirring in the shadows of the infamous star Betelgeuse, a cosmic poltergeist that is disrupting the atmosphere of the red supergiant. New radio observations have shown Betelgeuse's smaller stellar companion, Siwarha (not Betelguese Betelguese, unfortunately), cutting through the supergiant's extended atmosphere and leaving a wake in its path, like a jet boat slicing through a lake.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
